source.title: From superposition to sparse codes: interpretable representations in neural networks
source.authors: David A. Klindt; Charles O'Neill; P. Reizinger; Harald Maurer; N. Miolane

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports its own additivity measurements in ViT-B/16 image representations, extending the superposition idea to a visual model setting. It does not test the listed toy-model, LLM, or SAE-specific versions.
record.gate_note: Included the paper's own Figure 1 and Figure 3 additivity/analogy results. Theoretical discussion, compressed-sensing claims, and findings attributed to cited studies are not rows. The Figure 1 caption reports an aggregate N=10 significance result without per-example values.
record.test_reason: This is a perspective paper. Its only empirical content is an illustrative additivity and analogy demo in ViT-B/16 on a handful of images. That demo measures linear composition of image representations, not features outnumbering dimensions, non-orthogonal packing, capacity competition, or SAE recovery. It is therefore a related construct (linearity/additivity) and is recorded under fits_no_version. The rest of the paper is theory: identifiability, compressed-sensing bounds and a proposed pipeline. Its points on SAE limits (suboptimal recovery, non-universal features) cite other studies rather than report the paper's own results.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right but incomplete. The authors argue, as a perspective, that three steps explain superposition and provide a route to interpretable codes. First, identifiability theory (from cited work) implies that classification-trained networks recover latent variables up to a linear map. Second, compressed sensing and sparse coding can lift sparse features out of non-orthogonal superposition. Third, quantitative, permutation-invariant interpretability metrics should evaluate the extracted codes. They also flag SAE recovery limits, the binding problem, and non-Euclidean latents as open problems.
record.recipe_differences: The paper measures image-representation additivity and a neural analogy in ViT-B/16; it does not reproduce the original toy-model training setup or its geometry and sparsity sweeps.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports a contrast between neural representation space (p < 10^-5) and pixel space (p ≈ 0.88) for the further-example additivity test.

fits_no_version.finding: In ViT-B/16, the representation of a composite image approximates the sum of its component representations. This held over N=10 examples (p<10^-5 against an A-vs-B cosine baseline) but not in pixel space (p≈0.88). A single analogy (elephant + pink ball − ball ≈ pink elephant) gave cosine similarity 0.92.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Linear/additive composition of concepts in vision-model representations (linear representation hypothesis), as distinct from superposition.

record.problems: The reported aggregate test uses N = 10 further examples. The main examples are illustrated rather than numerically tabulated, and the paper does not test feature dimensionality, feature geometry, or SAE feature completeness in these experiments.

untested.parts: No toy models, sparsity sweeps, phase transition or feature geometry; the paper restates the idea only in theory (Definition 2, compressed-sensing bounds).
No test of capacity competition or of dedicated versus shared dimensions.
No test of non-capacity causes of polysemanticity.
No measurement of feature spread across neurons or of SAE recovery in any LLM. Figure 4 plots theoretical bounds, with cited models placed on them.
SAE suboptimal recovery and non-universality are argued from cited work (O'Neill et al. 2025; Paulo & Belrose 2025), not tested here.
Multi-dimensional and non-Euclidean features are mentioned only as an open limitation; there is no measurement.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T3' is downgraded to 'discusses/T6' for two reasons. The ViT demo is illustrative (N=10 unshown examples plus two figure panels). Its additivity measure does not bear on superposition as V1–V6 define it; the paper itself separates linearity (Definition 1) from non-orthogonal superposition (Definition 2). Toy Models of Superposition is cited and discussed, not tested.

versions.untested_parts: No toy networks with more sparse features than dimensions, sparsity-dependent transition, or regular feature geometry are tested.
No test of capacity pressure, feature importance, or neurons sharing versus receiving dedicated dimensions.
No test of alternative causes of polysemantic neurons or whether polysemanticity is evidence of superposition.
The measured model is ViT-B/16, not an LLM; the paper does not test feature spread across LLM neurons or SAE recovery in an LLM.
The paper discusses sparse coding and SAE limitations but does not itself test whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical.
No measurement tests whether represented features are one-dimensional rather than multidimensional.

rows.subject: ViT-B/16
rows.operation_detail: Compared the neural representation of a combined image with the representations of its component images.

conditions.value: GPT-4-generated elephant, pink ball, and combined elephant-and-pink-ball images

rows.measure: Cosine-similarity visualization for the additivity test
rows.note: The text describes the combined representation as approximated by the sum of the component representations; no numerical similarity value is stated for this panel.
rows.check: Figure-only scatter with no numeric value. 'Observed' is the reader's reading of the caption, not a value. Additivity is not a measure of superposition as any version defines it.

rows.subject: ViT-B/16
rows.operation_detail: Compared the neural representation of an image containing both animals with the representations of the two animals separately.

conditions.value: Real images of a dog (Hazel), a cat (Nemo), and both together

rows.measure: Cosine-similarity visualization for the additivity test
rows.note: The caption says additivity holds for these natural images; no numerical similarity value is stated for this panel.
rows.check: Figure-only with no numeric value. Additivity on one natural image pair is not a measure named by any version.

rows.subject: ViT-B/16
rows.operation_detail: Tested additivity over further image examples and compared the result with a calibrated baseline.
rows.measure: Statistical significance of additivity over the calibrated baseline
rows.baseline: Calibrated baseline: cosine similarity of the representations of A and B
rows.note: The caption reports this as an aggregate result over the further examples; it does not give per-example values.
rows.check: Aggregate over N=10 unshown examples, p<10^-5 against an A-vs-B cosine baseline. It bears only on additivity, not on any version.

rows.subject: pixel space (g)
rows.operation_detail: Compared pixel-space additivity with the calibrated baseline for further image examples.
rows.measure: Statistical significance of additivity over the calibrated baseline
rows.baseline: Calibrated baseline: cosine similarity of the representations of A and B
rows.note: The caption says the result was not statistically significant in pixel space.
rows.check: Pixel-space comparator (p≈0.88). Its subject is the input space, not a model. Keep it only as a control for r3.

rows.subject: ViT-B/16
rows.operation_detail: Measured a neural analogy using representations of elephant, pink ball, ball, and pink elephant images.

conditions.value: GPT-4-generated images described by the four concepts

rows.measure: Cosine similarity for the neural analogy
rows.note: The caption presents the example as showing concepts combining linearly for this local case.
rows.check: A single analogy example with cosine similarity 0.92 and no baseline. It is illustrative and shows a linear 'pink' direction, not superposition.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
